AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: Identification of factors interfering with adequate control of arterial hypertension in the course of antihypertensive therapy is necessary to plan the strategy or reducing the incidence of cardiovascular disorders and optimize clinical practice guidelines. There have only been limited reliable studies describing the current status of hypertension treatment.

AbstractText.Label: AIM
AbstractText.content: The study objective was to conduct a screening assessment of the rate of uncontrolled hypertension among hypertensive patients coming to a routine follow-up visit, and to characterize patients with inadequate control of arterial hypertension in the aspect of their cardiovascular risk profile and therapeutic strategies used.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: CONTROL NT registry was a nationwide non-interventional observational study performed by physicians in the outpatient setting in Poland. Patient data were collected twice: between April and September 2011 and between January and August 2012. Each physician conducted screening of consecutive patients with a history of arterial hypertension coming to a routine follow-up visit, until the selection of 10 patients with uncontrolled hypertension or inclusion of 50 patients. In the course of screening, the physician completed a form with basic information on the patient (gender, age, blood pressure measurement, primary risk factors, treatments used). In patients with inadequate control of arterial hypertension (defined as systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥ 140 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure (DBP) ≥ 90 mmHg measured in the office on the visit day), physicians collected additional data on medical history, physical examination, laboratory tests and current antihypertensive treatment (antihypertensive agents and their doses) and its modifications. The observation was supplemented by office blood pressure readings and details of treatment at the subsequent routine visit. The impact of the selected demographic and clinical parameters on treatment success defined as BP lowering to <140/90 mmHg when measured in the office at the second visit was investigated with univariate and multivariate logistic regression models.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: In total 1288 outpatient physicians participated in the CONTROL NT registry. In the screened group of 34,919 patients with a history of arterial hypertension, 66.9% had abnormal blood pressure readings in the office. In the group of 15,262 patients with inadequate control of hypertension included in further analysis, the mean age was 59.3 ± 11.9 years, 47.9% were women, the disease duration was 8.2 ± 6.5 years (median 7.0) and antihypertensive therapy was used for 7.4±6.0 years (median 6.0). Mean SBP and DBP values measured in the office on the visit day were 160 mmHg and 95 mmHg, respectively, and the mean heart rate was 78 bpm. At least 3 cardiovascular risk factors were found in 46% of patients. The most common were dyslipidaemia (77.4%) and abdominal obesity (74.8%). During the study, 24.4% of patients smoked cigarettes and 39.4% of patients reported smoking cessation in the past. Elevated body mass index (BMI) ≥ 25 kg/m² was found in 84.2% of study subjects and heart rate ≥ 70 beats per minute was found in 83.4% of study subjects. In 56.6% of patients at least one concomitant disease was diagnosed, the most common being diabetes (29.8%) and coronary artery disease (28.5%). At the time of inclusion into the study 21.5% of patients received no antihypertensive drugs, 16.8% received one drug, 28.5% two drugs in combination therapy, and 31.5% received three or more drugs. The most commonly used drug class was angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (50%), followed by beta-blockers (42%) and diuretics (39%). Fixed-dose combinations were received by 4% of patients. The modification of antihypertensive treatment prescribed after the first visit enabled obtaining blood pressure values <140/90 mmHg measured in the office at the subsequent follow-up visit in 60% of study subjects. Significant negative predictors of blood pressure control included elevated body mass index (BMI) ≥ 30 kg/m², increased heart rate ≥ 70 beats per minute, longer duration of hypertension ≥ 7 years and coexisting kidney disease (the odds ratios (OR) adjusted by age and gender were 0.61; 0.76; 0.79; 0.76, respectively).

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: The percentage of Polish outpatients receiving antihypertensive treatment who achieve adequate control of arterial hypertension is unsatisfactory. Patients with diabetes, chronic kidney disease, dyslipidaemia, overweight or obesity, longer disease and treatment duration and poor treatment compliance are expected to present a particular challenge in antihypertensive treatment. They require a particularly careful assessment of risk factors and comorbidities, appropriate therapy intensification and more frequent use of antihypertensive fixed-dose combinations.
